newsitem.title: INDIA: Gold - Indian budgetary scheme seen helping supply.
newsitem.headline: Gold - Indian budgetary scheme seen helping supply.

text.p: An Indian amnesty scheme, aimed at drawing out "black" or unaccounted money, could help boost gold supply in India, dealers and analysts said on Monday.
They said an improved supply in India could influence prices in the re-export markets such as Dubai, which mainly feeds on the demand from the Indian sub-continent, including Pakistan.
"A substantial quantity of black money goes into gold. People, who are holding gold, can now liquidate it and disclose the amount under the scheme," said analyst Madhusudan Daga.

The Voluntary Disclosure Scheme (VDS), aimed at tapping the unaccounted money that escaped the tax net, was announced on Friday by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his federal budget for 1997/98 (April/March).
Dealers said there were no any estimates of the amount of black money invested in gold.
The tax-friendly budget has been widely acclaimed as growth-oriented and is expected to spur incomes.
"The budget is like a double-edged sword," Daga said. "While the overall economic growth could boost demand for gold, part of the hoarded bullion could come out under the VDS."
In the week to Monday, gold prices rose 100 rupees per 10 grammes to 4,980 rupees on the Bombay bullion market.
Dealers said a firm world trend made imports costlier, affecting the availability of gold in the local market.
"Arrivals of imported gold are almost negligible," said leading jeweller Babubhai Jain. "The rising prices in the world market also triggered some speculative buying locally."
Dealers said the price of imported gold, exceeding 4,900 rupees per 10 grammes, inclusive of duties and other costs, left little or no profit margin.
"Near-term price trends depend on the world market," Jain said. "At present, the local market is overbought and a correction is on the cards."
Dealers in Pakistan's main commercial city of Karachi said gold prices would rise slightly in the current week on demand from jewellers.
One dealer said prices had been moving up for the past week on increased wedding season demand from jewellers.
In Dubai, dealers said physical demand for gold from their key markets of India and Pakistan remained subdued.

"The market is very crazy at the moment. It is running so high but there is low physical demand. Prices rose too high in a short period of time," said a dealer. "Demand from India and Pakistan is low and the Asian market is dull."
February witnessed strong demand and high turnover because of the Indian wedding season but traders said buying has since faded.
"The wedding demand is over and I expect the market to stay as it is for another week or so," said another dealer.
